inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: This type is a chain of four fixed filter sections and an output gain: a low shelf, two peaking sections that share one law, a high shelf. The low shelf is one pole and one zero, and so is the high one -- which the band profiles this was read from could not say, because they are magnitude and a second-order section differs from a first-order one in phase everywhere and in magnitude only past a corner this unit has no output beyond. Each parameter byte selects from a short table rather than driving a formula -- a gain answers over twenty-five values and sticks at both ends, a corner has two states, a width has five entries and returns the first for anything past them, a centre moves in equal steps of log frequency for every eighth value of its byte, at the named third octaves between the printed ends and at one entry that is not one of them.

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: This type is eight peaking sections parked at fixed centres, one output pan and one level, with a single width byte driving all eight instead of one each. The centres are the named third octaves at 250, 500, 1k, 1.25k, 2k, 3.15k, 4k and 8k: a band raised to the top of its byte and cut to the bottom returns the same centre to within 0.02 octaves, and the eight sit 0.030 octaves under the named series with a scatter of 0.018 -- which is the offset this unit's other equaliser's table was measured to carry. That offset has since been measured to be the unit's rather than the reading's, by putting a section of known centre through the same band set, window and fit at the width both types were read at, where it comes back on the name to two thousandths of an octave -- so the eight really do sit below the series they are named by. With each type's own mean taken out the seven centres the two types share still run the same way, over a pattern 0.046 octaves wide that they disagree about by 0.012 at worst and 0.006 in the median. Whether that is one table or two tables computed the same way is not separated here. The width byte indexes five entries and four of them are the equaliser's Q byte's entries exactly: 2.583, 1.417, 0.750 and 0.417 octaves between the half-gain points, on a reading whose step is a twelfth. Past the fifth printed step the two types disagree. This one returns the fifth entry and the equaliser returns the first, so what is shared is the table and not the handling of a byte outside it. Each band gain answers over the twenty-five values from 52 to 76 and returns the nearest end for everything outside, and the power-on state is the eight defaults its own page prints, read through a width byte the page prints no default for and which powers up at its third entry.
inferences.named: The eight band gains at 40 03 03 through 40 03 0A, the width byte at 40 03 0B and the pan at 40 03 15, on type 01 01.

inferences.why: the claim took its rounds and did not close
inferences.claim:
The byte a page prints `Drive` against sets how hard a signal is driven into a fixed nonlinearity. It does not choose between curves and it does not change the curve: over the settings the comparison can reach, feeding the stage a louder signal at one drive returns the same reading as raising the drive at one input, the reading being the level at each whole multiple of the carrier under the level at the carrier. That is a statement about the stage and not about the signal. If the stage is one curve behind one gain then scaling what it is fed has the same effect whatever it is fed, so all this needs is that both sides of every comparison were made on the same signal, which they were. It is worth saying what it therefore does not need, because the signal is not what the run took it for: the voice is two oscillators about twelve cents apart at nearly the same size, so it beats, and the stage was driven at a level that moved through each take rather than one that stood still. The correspondence survives that untouched. What is read at each multiple of the carrier does not, and nothing here is a harmonic series. The input each setting wants is what that setting's own value gives when it is read as a gain -- twenty times the log of it over 48, in decibels, and 48 is where the page rests the byte rather than an origin chosen here. From setting 8 to 48 the wanted input tracks that law to between a tenth and four tenths of a decibel, against bars of a tenth to four and four tenths that the ladder measures for itself by putting each of its own rungs back from the others. The tightest of those rows is setting 32, where the law is asked to a tenth of a decibel and answers to a tenth. Two bounds, both measured. The byte's bottom three settings return one state -- 0, 2 and 4 agree order for order inside the run's own repeats -- so whatever the byte is there it is not a gain, which would have to be three different ones. Above 48 every setting wants more input than the part can give, and the comparison says nothing about them rather than pinning them to the ladder's last rung. The other standalone drive type is a different curve and not the same one rested somewhere else. No state this type can be put in comes within seven and nine tenths of a decibel of any state of that one, against repeats that agree to two hundredths. What the stage is fed is not the carrier: a fixed filter stands in front of it, and what reaches the curve is a shaped version. The stage's small-signal gain at the carrier is 11.87 decibels at 110 hertz, 20.37 at 220 and 23.08 at 330 -- a tilt of 11.21 decibels, 8.50 of it in the first octave. The level the three were fed is one level: across all 10 rungs of the ladder the three carriers differ in what went into the stage by at most 0.10 of a decibel, which is the worst of the rungs and not a chosen one. And where the ladder stops moving the output, the carrier comes to rest at -39.84, -39.93 and -40.49 decibels -- a spread of 0.65, against a tilt of 11.21 going in. A filter after the curve would carry that tilt onto the ceiling, because a curve that limits puts out what it puts out and anything after it multiplies that; a filter in front changes only how much arrives, so three carriers rest at one level however differently they got there. The ceiling is flat and the gain is not, so the tilt is in front. None of this moves the law above. Feeding one carrier a louder signal at one drive still matches raising the drive at one input, because the filter is the same filter on both sides of every comparison and every comparison was made on one carrier. What it does move is what the curve is taken to be fed: the input a setting wants is the input at the part, and the input at the curve is that input through a filter nobody here has identified. Its shape is not read off these three points -- eight and a half decibels in the first octave is steeper than any one-pole can be, and that is the whole of what the spacing supports. The tilt is a floor rather than a figure, and errs the safe way: the gain at the lowest carrier is the same at the bottom three rungs and is therefore the small-signal one, while at the highest carrier the gain is already falling by the second rung, so the number read there is under that carrier's own small-signal gain and the distance between them is under the true distance.

**The curve does not run out of orders, and near zero it is not smooth.** The byte was swept again on the voice measured to be one component at this note, read to 32 orders, and the series was asked how it behaves high up. At the setting the page rests the type at, the odd orders fall 6.3 decibels an order from the 11th to the 23rd and then stop falling: from the 25th to the 31st they sit at -77 decibels under the first, where the rate the low orders set would have carried them to -109. What is there stands 31 decibels over that, 37 over the same order of the take routed past the effect, and 72 over the floor between the orders in its own take -- so it is neither the voice, nor the chain, nor a floor the reading is sitting on. Across those last four odd orders the series falls 2.6 decibels, which is a power of the order and not an exponential: a curve smooth on the scale of the signal loses its orders faster than any power, and that is the whole of what the two readings differed by. Which power is not settled here. A jump gives 1.9 decibels across these four orders and a kink in the slope gives 3.7, and the repeats of one setting in this record fail to agree by more than the difference between them. A step and a corner are both what the smooth reading was not, and telling them apart is a finer question than the one that was asked.

**Read at one setting of the byte and not across it.** What stands over a high order is what this same stage makes of the voice's other partials, which is bounded by driving a stand-in curve as hard as the unit is driven. Below the resting place the stand-in cannot be brought near the unit's low orders at all -- 11 decibels away at the worst -- so the bound it returns is a number about the stand-in. Above it the low orders match and the drive that matches them is hard enough that the stand-in's own high orders stand over everything the unit shows, which is a bound that admits nothing rather than a reading that failed. One setting is what this run reads, and it is the one the page rests the type at.
inferences.named: a linear pre-gain into a fixed curve. Nothing is named about the curve. It is not called memoryless, because every figure was read on one held tone at one frequency and that cannot tell a static curve from one with a state in it; and nothing is said about where it departs from linearity, because the signal it was read on is two beating oscillators and the shape of a curve cannot be taken off that. A name is the first part of a claim to be retracted, and one half of this one already was

inferences.why: the comparison was made and carries no verdict yet
inferences.claim: This type is eight first-order all-pass sections in series, summed with the dry signal rather than averaged with it, running at thirty-two kilohertz. One byte moves every section's corner together, which puts four cancellations in the audible band at fixed ratios read in the tangent of frequency -- so they crowd towards each other in hertz as the byte takes them up, and the top ones leave the band rather than staying four.
inferences.named: a phaser as the period built one: an all-pass ladder mixed back with the input

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: The byte beside this type's manual is the gain of a feedback loop closed around the all-pass cascade, and it is not a second mix and not a resonance inside the sections. A cascade passes everything at unit gain, so summing it with the dry signal reaches six decibels where the two arrive in phase and no further; the profile reaches 18.87 dB, which a sum would need nearly eight helpings of the cascade to do. What the loop puts there instead is a resonance between each pair of notches -- where the cascade comes back in phase with itself and the return adds up -- while the notches stay where the closed reading put them. Two further things about it are readable, one at each end of the band. The return arrives one sample late, which is what a part computing a sample at a time has no choice about, and the phase that costs is nothing at the bottom and half a circle at half the rate: at the top of the band it turns the highest resonance into the cancellation it would otherwise have been, which the unit does and an instantaneous loop does not. And the return will not carry the bottom of the band: the lowest resonance is largest at 105 Hz and has fallen thirteen decibels by 25, by more the harder the loop is driven and by nothing at all when the loop is open -- which puts one pole of a high pass inside the loop and nowhere else in the chain. The loop gains themselves are a readout of seventeen settings and no law is claimed on them. What the seventeen do settle is that there is something to claim: the gain moves at every one of them, and the two that share the top four bits of the byte come back 0.0675 apart -- further than any neighbouring pair of the sweep -- so this byte is not the sixteen-entry table the byte one address along on the same type turned out to be.
inferences.named: a feedback path around an all-pass cascade, a sample late and blocked at DC

inferences.why: the claim took its rounds and did not close
inferences.claim: A rotary's slow rate byte indexes the same printed table every other rate byte on this unit indexes -- the wide one, picked by the `0.05 - 10.0` the page prints against it, with no constant of its own anywhere in it. What the rotary adds is that the entry is where a rotor is sent and not where it ends up. Sent down, it arrives exactly -- which is measured and not inferred: the same byte written after a faster one, with no reset between, comes back on its entry where the same byte written after a reset comes back short of it. Sent up, it stops a fixed distance short: 0.245 Hz on the low rotor and 0.062 on the high, holding to a thousandth of a hertz from the corner to the top of the byte and across both places the table's own step changes. And where the distance to the entry is narrower than that, the rotor barely sets off, so five entries of the low rotor's table return one rate and the high rotor moves a fifth of an entry across the one entry of its own. The width of that flat stretch and the size of the gap are the same number, which is what separates this from a constant subtracted after a lookup: read the gap off the top of the sweep alone and it places the corner, which neither half of the fit was shown. The distance is set by the acceleration byte the page prints against each rotor, and the two rotors are one routine reached twice: at every one of nine settings of that byte the two gaps agree to a median of 2.8 per cent, so the four to one between them is the two defaults and not the two rotors. What that byte does is a claim of its own beside this one.
inferences.named: a first-order lag done with an arithmetic right shift, which underflows climbing and floors falling

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: A rotary's acceleration byte is read through its top four bits, and the sixteen entries that leaves are what the rotor's loop multiplies the difference by before shifting it. So the distance the rotor stops short of the rate entry it was aimed at is one constant divided by what the entry holds. What the entries hold is a sequence: the first ten count up, one through ten, and then they double -- twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight. 14 of the sixteen are readable and 12 of those land on that sequence inside what their own take told a rate apart to, with one constant over the whole table and nothing else fitted. The last one does not: it reads 168 where the doubling says 256, five times what the take resolves, and it is published as the number it is. The byte is not a shift count, which is what a four-bit acceleration invited: the distance does not halve per step of it, and the near-four between the two rotors' defaults is where those two defaults happen to sit in this table. The two rotors are one routine reached twice -- at nine settings of the byte their distances agree to a median of 2.8 per cent. And the constant, 0.9768 Hz, names the clock a fifth time by a route none of the other four used: it is a rate divided by a power of two, and at thirty-two kilohertz that power is 14.9996 while at forty-four and forty-eight no integer power comes within four tenths.
inferences.named: a four-bit acceleration that multiplies the difference before the shift

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: The rotary's speed switch decides which of the type's two high-rotor rate bytes the rotor follows, and it turns over between 63 and 64 rather than at the 0x7F the page prints against it. Below that it is the slow byte, at every one of the 8 settings asked there; at and above it the fast byte, at every one of the 5, and the two arms are 0.84 Hz and 9.94 Hz apart so nothing turns on a small difference. With the switch on the fast arm the fast byte moves the rotor over the same printed table the slow byte was closed on -- ten settings, none of them further from an entry than the arrival gap already measured -- and the slow byte stops moving it at all, sitting inside 0.0002 Hz across three settings that span the whole of its range. What the byte does not decide is the arrival: below where the rotor already was, the fast byte lands on its entry to two thousandths of a hertz, and above it the rotor stops short by the same six hundredths the slow byte stops short by. That is the sign the mechanism beside this one predicts -- a lag written as an arithmetic right shift underflows climbing and floors falling -- and nothing here was fitted to it. Both of the readings this left standing were asked and both fell. The turnover is the machine's rather than this type's: the other type that prints the parameter turns over between the same two settings, with the same two rates under it. And the arrival is not the byte's: the same setting of the same byte stops short when it is written a third of a second after the switch and lands on its entry when it is written two seconds after it, which places the rotor between 4.05 and 4.25 Hz at the shorter gap.
inferences.named: a two-state parameter decoded from the top bit of its byte, selecting which of two entries of one rate table a rotor is sent to

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: The filter a stereo flanger puts in front of itself and the filter a stereo chorus puts in front of itself are one section. Swept at every setting the chorus's was published at -- 15 of them across the two filter shapes the byte beside it offers -- the two types return the same skirt over a hundred and thirteen twelfth-octave bands to a median of 0.08 dB at worst, where those runs repeat themselves to 0.08 dB and where one step of the byte being swept moves the profile by at least 0.15 dB. The agreement is at the floor and the thing it is being told from is two to ten times the floor, so this is the reading saying the same section twice and not the reading running out. The page prints the two types' parameter lists identically -- same order, same addresses, same ranges -- with one entry in the flanger's that the chorus has not got, a feedback level in the slot the chorus leaves empty. That list is what made the question worth asking and it is not what answers it; what this file claims is the front end, and what the loop is around is queued. The byte the flanger has and the chorus has not is a loop, and it is around the delay the byte beside it sets. A loop around a delay has to do three things and none of them is what a filter does, so each was asked separately and the modulator was parked at no rate and no depth throughout so that the delay stood still while they were. It puts teeth in the spectrum: 23.4 decibels of them at the ends of the byte, against 0.79 dB at the centre the page prints as nought -- so the printed nought is no loop rather than a small one. It deepens them without moving them: across the three settings either side where the teeth clear the run's own repeats, the delay read off the comb does not move at all while the depth goes from a third of its range to all of it. And it spaces them by the delay the byte beside it sets, which is the one that says the loop is around that delay and not around some second structure: at pre-delay 6 the comb reads 0.618 ms and at 13 it reads 1.318, a ratio of 2.133 where the byte's own is 2.167. That is the same delay per step of the byte in both places, 0.1022 ms, read two ways that did not have to agree. The loop's sign is the cheapest confirmation of all and it is there: below the printed nought the teeth sit halfway between where they sit above it, which is what an inverting loop does and what nothing else does. Scored as an inverting comb the negative settings beat the same profile scored as an in-phase one by 1.59 times at worst, and the delay each sign returns is the other's to within the width of the reading. The two modulators are not one, and the depth byte is what says so. The run this file queued was made three times, at the pre-delay a comb read at six tenths of a millisecond, near each type's own printed default, and at three times that. Read properly the three agree with each other to 2.98 per cent at every setting, which is the point: the pre-delay does not enter a pitch excursion at all, and three runs that differ in nothing that could move it returning one curve is what says the curve is the byte's. The setting each was asked twice at repeats to 2.74 per cent. Both curves rise with their own byte at every step. And they are not the same curve: the flanger swings 12.9, 27.5, 61.1, 100.7, 147.2 cents where the chorus swings 9.8, 19.3, 39.9, 66.4, 98.1, a ratio running from 1.316 to 1.501. One stage reached twice returns one excursion; these differ at every setting by two orders of magnitude more than either repeats to, and they differ by a ratio that is not constant, so it is not a gain in front of one modulator either. The front end is shared and the modulator is not.

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: The byte type `01 24` prints `Step Rate` against is the clock of a sample and hold, and the byte it prints `Rate` against is the waveform that clock samples. Written to the bottom of its own printed table, where the page reads 0.05 Hz and a cycle does not fit inside a take, the step byte stops the flanger moving at all: the partial level swing is the bypassed take's three tenths of a decibel, and the period the reading returns at four of six settings of the other byte is 4.79 to 4.82 Hz, which is this voice's own amplitude wobble and not the effect. With that clock running at a printed 2.00 Hz instead, the other byte returns its own printed table to four figures -- 0.4997, 0.9995 and 1.9987 Hz where the page prints 0.50, 1.00 and 2.00 -- and above the clock it returns what sampling predicts rather than what the page prints: a printed 5.00 comes back at 0.9996, which is its distance from twice the clock. Read the other way round, with the sampled byte held at a printed 1.00 Hz and the step byte swept over a factor of twenty, the output repeats at 0.9994 to 0.9997 Hz at every setting of the clock at or above that rate and never at the clock's own. A period that follows the sampled byte and not the clock, a clock that freezes the stage when it stops, and an alias where the sampled byte runs faster than the clock are the three things a hold does and the three things two modulators reaching one delay do not.

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: A filter byte's corner sits on a single pole, and both filters this type's type byte selects are one pole each. The low pass falls six decibels an octave through the middle of the band and the high pass the same the other way; neither is a biquad and neither is two poles cascaded, which would be twelve. The low pass carries the zero the bilinear transform leaves at half the rate, and that is what makes a clock readable off it: the skirt bends from 5.7 decibels an octave between 800 Hz and 1.6 kHz to 10.3 between 6.4 and 12.7 kHz, which puts half the rate just above the top of the band and the rate at thirty-two kilohertz. Read at forty-four or forty-eight it is four times worse and leans. The high pass names the order and cannot name the rate: its corners are all under 500 Hz, its zero is at nothing, and the place a warp would show is its own flat passband. One corner table serves both -- at the four settings both were read the two agree to within 0.064 octaves, which is what this reading resolves.
inferences.named: a one-pole section, the same one written twice with its numerator changed

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: A delay's damping byte is one pole inside the delay's own feedback loop, and it is the pole written the cheapest way there is: a running average, one multiply and one state, with no zero at half the rate. Inside rather than once on the way out, which is read off how a held note builds: with the byte at the position the page prints as the filter out the build is 18.3 dB and it is the same in every band, and with the filter in it falls away above a frequency that moves more than four octaves across the byte. A filter outside the loop is the same shape in both windows and cancels between them. That is not the section the same part's chorus filter byte sits on. A pole put through the bilinear transform keeps a zero at half the rate and its skirt bends steeper as it climbs towards it; this one has no zero, so its skirt stops cutting and levels off -- and the profile does level off, on every one of the ten settings the run asked, at a different depth each time. Where a profile levels off names the pole outright with nothing fitted, because the depth is one minus the coefficient over one plus it. Scored through the same takes the cheap pole is sixteen times the bilinear one's median and is the only candidate of eight whose residual does not lean. And it names the clock a fourth time, by a route none of the first three used: the coefficient that puts the corner where the page prints it depends on the rate, so a corner fitted freely from each setting's own skirt lands on the printed third octaves to a five-hundredth of an octave at thirty-two kilohertz and a twentieth at forty-four -- high at every setting, which is a lean and not a scatter. Read on two more types the same byte does one of two things. On the modulated delay it is the same byte doing the same thing: over ten settings and a hundred and thirteen bands the two profiles sit a median 0.045 dB apart, which is under what either run failed to repeat, and the corners agree to a fifteenth of an octave. Nothing was refitted for it -- the claim was closed on one type and reproduced on a second it had never seen. Inside the chorus-and-delay pair it is not. There the profiles sit a median 10.04 dB apart, and the shape is the thing that differs rather than the depth: on both delays the skirt is still falling at the top of the band, by 10.15 dB over the last two octaves at the byte's bottom, while in the pair it has flattened to -0.08 and sits at -24.38 dB from two kilohertz upward. Two explanations for that were tried and both are refused. It is not the run's floor: restricted to the bands where each setting's own take stands twelve decibels clear of its own silence the disagreement is still 10.04 dB. And it is not the held block meaning different things -- the delay time and the feedback on all three types are printed on one conversion column and one hex range, so the same byte is the same quantity, and what differs in the print is each type's own default. What the pair's profile is, is not read here. The claim is a claim about one slot and it now has one type it reaches and one it does not.
inferences.named: a one-multiply pole, the running average a fixed-point part damps a delay's repeats with

inferences.why: the claim took its rounds and did not close
inferences.claim: Type `01 60`'s pitch bytes are not read by anything that runs at a rate of its own. They are read out of a window, and the output repeats every time the read-out has drifted that window's length -- so the rate a take carries is `|r - 1| / T`, where `r` is the ratio the two pitch bytes ask for and `T` is the window. Across the coarse byte the ratio was moved from a quarter to double, which is `|r - 1|` from 0.056 to 1.000, and the rate moved with it from 0.90 to 15.63 Hz: over that factor of eighteen `T` stays between 62.1 and 64.7 ms. At unison the line is not slow, it is gone -- byte 64 returns 4.81 Hz, which is this voice's own amplitude wobble and the same figure the fine byte returns at its own unison. On the fine byte, which reaches ratios three orders closer to one than the coarse byte's smallest step does, the four settings whose implied rate clears the run's own floor of 0.3033 Hz come back at 0.4504 to 0.9384 Hz and give `T` of 63.21 to 63.74 ms, while every setting between them returns the voice's wobble instead -- which is what a window rate under the floor looks like and is not something a clock of the stage's own could do. The byte the page prints `Shift Mode` against, over five states and with no unit beside them, moves `T` and moves nothing else. Its five states return 32.00, 42.68, 63.78, 85.27 and 128.0 ms, which is the ratio 3 : 4 : 6 : 8 : 12, read at two shifts an octave apart. The shortest is 1024 steps of the 32000 Hz clock this archive already reads this unit's delay ladder as cut to; the third is 2048 of them and the fifth is 4096, so three of the five are successive powers of two and the two between them sit a fourth and a fifth along -- two octaves reached in four steps. Read at the octave, where the two shortest windows put the rate past the 20 Hz ceiling this reading searches to, those two and only those two come back at exactly half: 15.6261 where 31.25 is asked for, and 11.7221 where 23.44 is.
inferences.named: a time-domain splicer: one window read out at the pitch ratio and re-entered every time the read-out has drifted the window's length, with a mode byte that picks which of five windows is used

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: Type `01 61`'s mode byte picks a length, and the five it picks stand in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6 : 8 : 12 -- the ratio the single pitch shifter's five windows were measured to stand in. Read as the distance the output holds a copy of itself at, with the shifter two semitones up where four takes of one state land 0.021 ms apart, the five states give 28.505, 38.000, 57.000, 75.995 and 114.026 ms -- against the first state 1.000, 1.333, 2.000, 2.666 and 4.000 where the ratio predicts 1, 1.333, 2, 2.667 and 4, every one of them inside that 0.021. At unison the same five land up to 10.52 ms apart from themselves, five hundred times further, so the reading the ratio rests on is the shifted one and the unison takes bound nothing. Each distance is 0.8906 of the window at the same state, to four figures across all five, and that multiple is not explained here.

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim:
The byte printed `Lo-Fi Type 1 - 6 - 9` at `40 03 04` on type `01 72` is not one quantity with nine values. It is two fields of one byte, and the two are told apart by where they show rather than by any arithmetic on the index.

**What the low field does is hold the signal for a whole number of samples.** Read with the type's own filters parked where they were measured to pass the most, the nine entries are three behaviours each appearing three times, grouped by the index modulo three: inside a group the profiles agree to 0.34 dB at the median against a floor of 0.25 dB, and the nearest two entries from different groups differ by 0.66 dB. One group is flat. The second puts a null 19 dB deep at 10679 Hz and the third one 26 dB deep at 8000 Hz, and all three entries of each group put it in the same band. A null is what holding a sample for a whole number of periods does and a low pass table is not: the third group's profile comes back up after its null and goes down again at the top of the band set, which is a second null where a hold of four samples has to have one and where nothing with one corner does.

**And the two nulls measure the rate rather than assuming it.** They stand in the ratio 1.3348, which is 5.0 bands of this set apart and is four to three to inside one of them. Read as a hold of three samples and a hold of four, they imply a rate of 32036 Hz and 32000 Hz -- two numbers this record produces independently of each other, agreeing to a tenth of a per cent, and agreeing with the 32000 Hz this archive reads on classes that share none of these takes.

**What the high field does is not visible in a signal that fills the path.** At full level the index divided by three changes nothing: entries six, seven and eight sit on top of entries nought, one and two to inside the floor. Read through the narrowest entry of the type's own pre filter, which is thirty decibels down, the last three entries stand 7.6 dB louder than the first six while the first six stand together. Something that adds to a quiet signal and not to a loud one is what this reading can say; which of the things that do is not read here.

**What the high field does is quantise.** The three entries were asked as orders of a held tone rather than as bands, at three levels of one stimulus spanning 36.1 decibels at the effect's own input, with the low field flat so that no hold was putting energy where an order would be read and the type's own filters left where they pass the most. Above the thirteenth order, the last entry stands 38 to 42 decibels over the first while the floor between those same orders rises only 21 to 30. The lift is 11 to 17 decibels more on the orders than between them, so what is added sits on whole multiples of the stimulus and is not a floor under it. A noise source at a fixed level puts nothing on the orders; a quantiser working on a periodic signal puts all of it there, because its error repeats with the signal.

**And it does not follow the signal down.** Read against the converter rather than against the first order, the added series sits at -84 to -87 decibels across the whole 36.1 decibels of input, which is a step fixed in the signal's own units and not a proportion of it. Against the tone it is therefore loudest where the tone is quietest, which is what the band profile saw as a lift that only shows on a quiet signal.

**Two of the field's three values are one value.** Its first and second differ by at most 6.2 decibels over these orders, against repeats of one setting that themselves fail to agree by 13.1 at the closest of the three levels: the two settings are nearer to each other than the run can separate, and the whole of the lift is the third value by itself. What the page prints as nine entries is a hold with three values and a quantiser with two.
inferences.named: a sample-and-hold rate in the low field of a byte, and something else in the high

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: Two of this type's four filters are printed on one conversion column, and the unit returns one table through both of them. The column's fifteen frequencies are the third octaves from 250 Hz to 6.3 kHz with a sixteenth entry that is the filter switched out, and read on the generator's own low pass the corners land a median 0.018 octaves off the printed entry and never more than 0.065 -- 19 per cent of one step of the column, over 16 readings of its 15 entries. The disc generator's low pass, a different byte on the same column inside the same type, returns the same corners to a median 0.053 octaves, and 15 of 16 land inside what that sparser source failed to repeat at the corner being read. Both are one pole. Rendered onto the same band set and read by the same corner reader, a single pole falls -2.97 decibels an octave at its own corner and -5.60 past it, where a pair falls -5.86 and -11.94; the generator low pass measures -3.10 and -5.90, and the disc low pass -3.05 and -5.90. The eight-value quantum is readable from inside one run rather than assumed: settings 8 and 15 fall in one printed entry and return corners 0.0018 octaves apart, while setting 0 one entry below returns one 0.415 octaves away -- a ratio of 237. What the same run says about the third filter is a negative and a structural one. The type's own filter, at 40 03 05 on the neighbouring column, moved the generators' output by no more than 0.54 decibels at any of eighteen settings and across its own off switch, on takes repeating to 0.04 decibels and standing 52 decibels over the run's silence -- material the same reader pulled 49.5 decibels of filter out of one byte away. The noise generators are not behind that filter.
inferences.named: one sixteen-entry corner table, read by two one-pole sections

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim:
The rotary on `11 07` and the rotary on `03 00` are the rotary of `01 22`, above the settings where the rotor being read is still on its way -- which is value 16 on the low rotor and 17 on the high, and not one boundary for both. `01 22` prints ten rotary parameters at `03` through `0B` and then, after an address no page names at `0C`, at `0D`; `11 07` prints the same ten at `08` through `10` and then `11`, with nothing between, so nine of them move five addresses and the tenth moves four. Swept on both and laid over each other, from value 16 to the top of the byte the two are 0.6 cents apart at worst -- across both places the shared table folds, at both take lengths the single type was read at, and at value 32 which was taken at both lengths as the tie. This is the third pair of a multi and its single-effect sibling to be asked and the first read by a stage that recovers a frequency rather than a level, so the agreement is not something a band reading could have manufactured. A third type carries the same ten at `0A` through `12` and then `13` -- nine move seven addresses and the tenth six, a third renumbering and the first read with a drive standing in front of the block rather than a branch beside it. Both of its rotors were swept and laid over the single type's own records: out of transit it stands within 0.74 cents of the single type, and at five of the thirteen settings asked out of transit the two return the same number to four decimal places. The widest any two of the three stand apart is 1.35 cents, between the two multis at value 32 -- the one setting taken at both take lengths, where each type disagrees with itself by as much (1.11 cents on the single type and 1.35 on this one). That is the floor two take lengths put under the comparison and not a distance between the types.

Below value 16 the two disagree by as much as 1507.2 cents, and this says nothing about either block. The same byte at the same value on the same type returns three different rates depending on how many bytes the run wrote before it -- 0.5934 Hz at value 12 after two writes, 0.5472 after three, 0.4042 after thirteen, which is what the multi returns after three and after nineteen. Down there a reading is of the byte and to when the write arrived, and neither record states it.

The high rotor answers the same way and the distance is not one number. The pair's other rotor was read on both types in one run, at one settle, with each type's other rotor silenced, and at the three settings both were asked it returns the same rate to between a tenth and a third of a cent. Its distance short of the printed entry is 0.056 to 0.061 Hz on both, agreeing to between a ten-thousandth and thirteen ten-thousandths of a hertz -- a second quantity the table does not contain, at a second address pair. And it is not an unrelated second quantity: the low rotor's distance over this one is 4.00 at the setting where the shared rate table steps by a twentieth of a hertz, and 4.19 and 4.39 at the two where it steps by a tenth and a half, against the 4.00 the two entries of this unit's own acceleration table give for the two bytes both types rest those rotors at. The drift is ordered the way the table's coarseness is, and the distance is read against that table.
inferences.named: one rotary, reached through a renumbering that is not a shift

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim:
The phaser half of `11 08` is the phaser of `01 20`, rather than a second one built to the same description. The page prints the two types' first five parameters at the same five addresses, with the same five printed ranges, the same two conversion columns and the same five printed defaults. Two of those five were swept on the multi at exactly the settings the single type's records were taken at and under the hold those records were taken under, and the profiles are the same profiles. What separates two phasers is where they put their cancellations, and where a cancellation sits is a thing that moves when the byte moves -- so the difference between the two records is split into the part that depends on the setting and the part that does not, and only the first of them could be a difference between two blocks. Over the 97 bands this stimulus reaches, the part that depends on the setting is 0.041 dB at the median and 0.77 dB at its worst, against the 23.9 to 33.4 dB the byte itself commands over those same bands: 32 times under the smallest thing it does. A corner table that differed anywhere would have to hide inside that. The part that does not depend on the setting is 0.043 dB at the median, and it is not read here as a difference between the two phasers because the two chains are not the same chain: the single type carries a pair of tone controls at the centre of their range in the path and the multi carries none at that address at all. The largest raw differences in the whole comparison are not at the notches, where a reader would look for them -- they are at 39 Hz and below, in the 16 bands at the bottom of the set where the runs cannot tell one of their own takes from another by better than a decibel and a half. **And the type is two branches summed rather than two stages in series.** Each half carries its own level byte. With the wah half's at nothing the output stands 56.8 dB above this run's own silence against 57.5 dB with both halves up, and with the phaser half's at nothing what is left still stands 45.2 dB above it -- where two stages in series would leave nothing, whichever of the two bytes were the chain's own output level. A second pair was asked and came back neither way. The reading left standing here named a run -- the flanger's feedback byte on `02 0A` against `01 23`, a pair whose page renumbers the block two addresses down instead of lining it up -- and it was made. Where the two profiles agree they agree where a comb is decided: nine of the ten settings put teeth in the band set, and 89 of the single type's 101 teeth land in the same band as a tooth of the multi's -- at the two settings whose combs are shallowest and cleanest, every one of the eleven does, at 749, 1498, 2245, 2997, 3776, 4490, 5339 Hz and on up, so the delay line and the length it is set to are shared. Where they differ they differ by more than the phaser pair ever did: the part that depends on the setting is 0.187 dB at the median and 3.4 dB at its worst, against the 5.4 dB the byte commands at the weakest setting it actually does anything at -- a factor of two and a half where the phaser pair returned thirty-two. **And this run cannot say what the difference is.** Two of the single type's bytes have no counterpart on the multi: a pre filter, which its records held off and which this type does not have, and a phase byte, which its records held at nought and which nothing on this type reaches. A flanger run at a different fixed phase returns a comb in the same places and not the same depths, which is what is measured. So the reading that the machine builds a multi out of its blocks is supported where it can be checked and is not closed, and what would close it is a pair with nothing held that the multi cannot be asked to hold too.

Both halves of one multi reach their single types' blocks. The wah half was then asked the same way and answers the same way, which is the thing the first round listed first among what it did not settle. Its manual byte moves a band-pass across 1.83 octaves on both types, and the two put the peak in the same twelfth-octave band at eight of nine settings and one band apart at the ninth -- which is the closest a band reading can place two things. Where the stage found a width to fit a curve over, the two corners land between a thousandth and six hundredths of an octave apart. Split the same way the phaser was, the part of the difference that depends on the setting is a tenth of a decibel through the middle of the range and runs between eighteen and fifty times under what the byte commands at that same setting. Both halves of one multi are therefore the single types' blocks, reached at addresses neither type prints them at together, and the wah's are five higher than the wah's own.

A second multi reaches the same wah block. `11 06` puts an overdrive where `11 08` puts a phaser and prints the wah's seven parameters at the same seven addresses, and its corner lands where the other two land: eight of nine settings in the same twelfth-octave band as the single type, the ninth one band away, and where the stage found a width to fit a curve over, seven thousandths of an octave apart. Against the first multi it is seven of nine and three thousandths. The part of the difference that depends on the setting is 0.13 dB at the median and runs between thirteen and forty-two times under what the byte commands at that same setting. Three types therefore reach one auto wah, two of them multis assembled out of different pairs, and the block is the block rather than one type having been built out of the single ones.
inferences.named: one phaser and one auto wah, both reached from a type that is neither

inferences.why: the claim took its rounds and did not close
inferences.claim: The delay a type prints `FL Dly` against and the loop it prints `FL Fb` against are, in all six types that print them inside a larger chain, the delay and the loop of the stereo flanger that stands alone. Read as a comb at two settings of the delay byte and on both signs of the loop, 23 of the 24 readings return the single type's figures exactly and the remaining one is refused by its own record's admission rule rather than disagreeing: 0.618 ms at a delay byte of 6 and 1.318 ms at 13 with the loop in phase, 0.624 and 1.296 with it inverted. That holds where the chorus runs into the flanger, where it sits beside it, where an overdrive or a distortion runs into it with no way out of the path, where an enhancer does, and where the flanger itself runs into a delay -- so no arrangement carries a delay line of its own, and on the last of them the pair of bytes is not even at the same address. The teeth are 21.91 dB deep at the shallowest admitted, and each is judged against its own record's bar rather than a shared one -- 10.20 to 22.89 dB across the six, cleared by 1.10 times at the nearest. Each profile scores as a comb of that spacing by at least 1.51 times what the same profile scores read on the other sign -- which is the control a filter sitting somewhere cannot imitate, since a peak scores the same either way. The modulator behind that delay is the single type's too, on the type the chorus runs into it. Its rate byte returns a table over ten settings whose four published ones are the single flanger's to four figures -- 1.6499 against 1.65, 4.9994 against 4.9993, 6.1007 against 6.0974, 9.9991 against 9.9986 Hz -- and the settings between them fall on the same line. Its depth byte buys the single flanger's excursion at every setting either run reads, to within 1.71 per cent against the 0.42 per cent one setting taken twice repeats to. On the type the chorus sits beside, the modulator is not read here: the reading that returns a rate picks a period out of an autocorrelation, and on that type the frequency series of a partial stands taller at twice the rate than at it at most settings of the flanger's feedback byte and carries nothing at the rate at all at the centre of it, which is where every run that is not asking about the loop parks that byte.

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: The byte a page prints `Small/BltIn/2-Stk/3-Stk` against is one table of four fixed responses, written once and reached from more than one place, and it sits after the drive stage rather than shaping what goes into it. One table, because an entry read on a type that is nothing but a drive stage and the same entry read from inside a pair land a median 0.18 dB apart across a hundred and thirteen twelfth-octave bands, where the same reading puts two different entries of the table 1.96 dB apart or more -- so the reading separates the entries by better than an order of magnitude over what it says separates these. After the drive stage, because the pair was read once with each of the two drive characters its selector offers, and those characters put out measurably different spectra: a median 3.87 dB apart in shape and 9.99 dB at their widest, one carrying nine decibels more above eight kilohertz and the other seven more through the midrange. A filter shaping the input to a nonlinearity does not divide out of the result, because the nonlinearity remaps whatever spectrum it is given; a filter after one does, exactly. The ratio between two amp entries is 0.09 dB apart between the two characters, which is under the runs' own repeats -- so it divides out, and the filter is on the output. The switch beside the byte is what puts the table in the path at all: at Off the profile is its own reference to a median of a seventh of a decibel, and at On it is a bandpass, 10.7 dB down through the bottom octave and 3.2 down above eight kilohertz against 4.9 up through the two to four kilohertz octave. Read in five more places the table holds and in a sixth it does not. The bass multi-effect is the one place that does not reach it. Driving the stage at 4 and at 127 rather than the 48 the first run held moves each entry's response by a median 0.165 and 0.18 dB -- a thirty-two-fold change in the drive byte, against a reading that puts two entries of the table 2.3 dB apart. The two families the first run could not reach return the same four as well: the stage followed by a chorus at 0.2 dB and the same stage as one of five in a guitar chain at 0.22, both at the same three entries and on the same band set. So one table is reached from three families, two printed shapes, at three different parameter numbers, and at three drive amounts spanning almost the whole byte. The bass multi is the exception and it is not a close one: its first three entries sit a median 7.7 dB from the same three read anywhere else, which is wider than the table's own entries are from each other, and its fourth setting -- the one its row prints no name against -- returns its reference to 0.13 dB while sitting 7.81 dB from the entry below it. Not the third entry repeated, not the fourth the other rows return, and not refused: the first entry, which is what the byte would give if its top value did not reach the table. The bass type was then asked which side of its own drive stage it sits on. Its own table sits after its own stage, so this unit has two of them and not one. Its entries move by a median 0.13 dB when the drive byte goes to 4 and 0.24 when it goes to 127, against its own entries sitting 6.41 dB from each other -- 27 times the larger of the two. So the one type that reaches different curves reaches them the same way the other five do, and the reading that would have made the disagreement an artefact of where the filter sits is refused. What is left is the plainest arrangement and not the cheapest one: two tables, one of four responses for the guitar-side types and one for the bass, each written after the nonlinearity it is heard through.
inferences.named: a fixed cabinet response, one short filter per entry, multiplying the drive stage's output

inferences.why: the comparison was made and carries no verdict yet
inferences.claim: An azimuth byte does not scale an angle and does not have 128 values. Two is added to it, the result is shifted right two places, the centre is taken off, and what is left is stopped at 15 either way -- so the byte reaches 31 positions 12 degrees apart, from L180 through 0 to R180. The added two is the rounding of a divide by four and nothing else: without it every position would sit a byte off the one the page prints. Twenty nine of the positions are 4 byte values wide and the two poles are 6, which is not a widening of those positions but the clamp taking the two values at each end of the byte the shift would have carried past them. The two poles are one place: half a turn to the left is half a turn to the right, and the page writes that into both cells rather than leaving it to be noticed.

inferences.why: the comparison was made and carries no verdict yet
inferences.claim: A byte printed `D> 0E - D 0<E` is two multipliers, each of them the byte's distance from a corner divided by fifty, truncated onto a grid of a hundred and twenty-eight and clamped at both ends -- and the two are offset so that they meet at full rather than crossing. The half that goes past the effect holds at its dry-end level for every setting up to and including 64, leaves it at 65, and is at nothing from 114 on. Read every count over both corners, thirty-two settings land within a sixth of a step of `min(1, floor((114 - n) * 128 / 50) / 128)` on the ramp and within half a step anywhere, and each of the three numbers in it is pinned by the reading: a quarter of a count on the width costs six times the residual, rounding instead of truncating costs seven times it, and the multipliers sit a twelfth of a step from the grid's entries where a number on no grid would sit a quarter of one away. Read in the window the return arrives in, the effect's own half rises for the last time at 64 and holds from 65, ten times what the takes repeat either way, so it is the direct half reflected through 128 rather than through 127: `min(1, floor((n - 14) * 128 / 50) / 128)`, whose corner and the direct half's sum to 128, and which meets the direct half at full at exactly 64. That half is read on two of the three types and carried by a shape rather than a threshold: truncation makes the four steps over the corner uneven, and reflected through 128 they are predicted at 0.220, 0.144, 0.211 and 0.206 of a decibel and read within 0.010 of that on one type and 0.031 on the other, where reflecting through 127 is out by 0.200 and 0.175. So the middle of the byte carries both halves at once and stands three decibels over either end, which is the opposite sign to a crossfade and not flat. Both ends reach true nothing: the direct window at the effect end falls to 1.1 decibels over the same take's own lead, which is the interface and not the unit. The law was found on one type at one count and holds on the two others, read at eight counts on a different day, to seven tenths of a step.
inferences.named: min(1, floor((114 - n) * 128 / 50) / 128) past the effect and min(1, floor((n - 14) * 128 / 50) / 128) through it, which is the same law reflected through 128 rather than through 127, so the two meet at full at 64

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: Every effect parameter this unit powers up holding is a value its own manual prints as that parameter's default. 575 parameters across sixty-five types were in a position to disagree and none did, 154 of them at a byte the printing leaves no choice about.

inferences.why: rejected
inferences.claim: A frequency byte does not drive a formula and does not have a hundred and twenty-eight values. Its top four bits index a table of sixteen entries, so eight settings share each entry, and the entries are the named third octaves between the two frequencies the page prints against that address -- with one that is not. On 200 - 6.3k, fifteen of the sixteen sit within 0.07 octaves of 200, 250, 400, 500, 630, 800, 1k, 1.25k, 1.6k, 2k, 2.5k, 3.15k, 4k, 5k and 6.3k, a median 0.03 and under what a twelfth-octave reading resolves. The third entry sits at 279 Hz where the series says 315, which is 0.18 octaves and two bands, and it is the only entry the reading and the series disagree about. Both mid sections return that same 279, and they return the whole of the first four entries to within 0.002 octaves of each other, so the two index one table rather than two. Read across its own eight settings the entry does not move -- 279.1, 278.7, 278.8 and 279.0 at 16, 17, 20 and 23 -- and the settings either side of it return the entries either side, so the stride is eight and the number in the table is 279.
inferences.named: a third-octave coefficient table indexed by the byte's high nibble, with one entry that is not a third octave

inferences.why: rejected
inferences.claim: A gain byte printed -12 - +12 is decibels, one per step, offset by sixty-four. It answers over a window of twenty-five values from 52 to 76 and returns the nearest end for everything outside. And the two of them that forty-three types carry with no frequency printed beside either are this unit's equaliser's own shelf pair with the frequency byte taken away and pinned to its first printed entry.

inferences.why: breaks_down
inferences.claim: An insertion effect's output level byte is a multiplier stored as a whole number over a hundred and twenty-seven, and that multiplier is not the byte. Every one of the hundred and twenty-five settings the run could read returns a gain that sits on the 1/127 grid: a median 0.0225 of a step away, against 0.2185 for the next best denominator of the sixty-one asked and 0.25 for a number that sat on no grid at all. What the entries are is a curve and not a formula -- the multiplier is three quarters of the byte over the bottom quarter of the range and rises to the byte itself at the top, and no law in the catalogue crosses that. The byte read straight as the multiplier is out by a median 1.61 decibels and by 3.53 at setting 9.
inferences.named: a stored table of seven-bit multipliers, one per setting

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim:
`Pre Filter 1 - 2 - 6` at `40 03 03` and `Post Filter 1 - 2 - 6` at `40 03 05` sit on one type, one on each side of its degrader, and are printed with the same name ending over the same range and the same six byte values. **They are two tables.**

**What the pre filter holds is a gain ladder with one stage switched across it.** Five of its six entries are three rungs 5.99 dB apart, and the rungs are gains rather than shapes: over the bands this reads they are the same number in every band to within 0.53 dB, against 0.62 dB from the same six entries swept twice in two sessions, and they tilt by 0.04 dB per octave at worst over six of them. The odd entries carry one stage and the even entries carry it with something else added, and the something else is the same curve both times: the step from entry one to entry two and the step from entry three to entry four agree to 0.16 dB at the median and 0.69 dB at worst. Entry nought is not a fourth rung: it stands 17.13 dB under entry one with a spread of 1.76 dB and a tilt of -0.27 dB per octave, both outside what the floor produces, so it is a different shape and not the bottom of the ladder.

**And what that stage is, is a notch and not a low pass.** It falls to -8.20 dB at 8000 Hz and comes back to nothing above it, reaching a quarter of a decibel of flat again by fifteen kilohertz -- which a corner cannot do and a dip in the middle of the band can. Fitted as a second order notch with its centre, its sharpness and its depth all free, the centre lands at 8000 Hz (Q 0.42, 0.61 of the way to a full null, residual 0.146 dB), and moving the centre five hundred hertz either way more than doubles that residual. **That stage is one tap added at two samples.** Held out a half of the band set at a time, the tap predicts the bands it was not shown to 0.44 and 0.31 dB while the freely centred section misses them by 2.33 and 3.25 -- and the section's centre lands at 9300 Hz from one half and 5550 Hz from the other, so the range as a whole is what was placing it. Rendering both through the band energies the unit was read as, rather than sampling them at the band centres, moves either curve by at most 0.042 dB and changes nothing. **8000 Hz is a quarter of 32000 Hz**, which is the clock this archive reads on classes that share no takes with these -- a delay ladder, a degrader's own two nulls -- and which nothing in this fit was told.

**What the post filter holds is not that.** The same three rungs, asked the same way, are shapes and not gains: they spread 2.90 to 2.96 dB where the pre filter's spread 0.31 to 0.53. The same alternation is there and its stage agrees with itself just as well (0.20 dB), but it is a different stage: deepest at 132 Hz where the pre filter's is deepest at 8000 Hz, with nothing below it coming back, and the two differ from each other by 5.28 dB at the median against a floor of 0.15. The entry that passes the most is the last of one byte and the first of the other.

**So a rule closed on one of them does not reach the other**, and the two are indistinguishable to anything reading the printed page: same last word, same range, same hex values, same type.
inferences.named: A gain ladder with a notch switched across it, and a shelf table -- two tables under one printed name.

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: The byte a 3D type prints `Speaker/Phones` against does not switch an output on or off and does not change a level. It picks between two renderings of the same placement, and which rendering is in use changes how the two channels are separated as a function of frequency. On the median plane the two renderings are the same thing: at the front and directly behind, where the placement leaves the two channels level, every one of a hundred and thirteen twelfth octaves agrees to within two tenths of a decibel and so does the total. Everywhere else they differ, and the difference turns over with frequency -- the speaker rendering separates the channels more below a hundred and twenty five hertz and less above two kilohertz, at 24 of the 24 placements that can show it -- every one of them -- and by up to 13.8 decibels in a band. The speaker rendering is also about a decibel and a half louder over the two channels together. The whole of it is antisymmetric about the front: the placement on one side returns the negative of its mirror to within 2.6 dB at the worst of 15 pairs, which is what says this is a property of the byte and the placement rather than of the takes. The same four are returned by the other type that places by a byte, read after the placement it names has arrived, so this is what the stage does and not what one type does.
inferences.named: output-mode

inferences.why: rejected
inferences.claim: A byte printed `L63 - 0 - R63` is one multiplier a side, the same pair on types whose front halves have nothing in common, and what stops it twenty-five decibels short of silence is not the multiplier. Read one band at a time the two channels separate by 33.7 decibels more in some bands than in others at the ends of the sweep and alike in all of them through the middle, against the same pair of channels with the effect taken out of the path separating alike everywhere to 0.1 of a decibel. A pair of multipliers has no frequency in it and cannot do that. Allow one term added after the pan and nineteen settings of twenty bands come back as one multiplier each, over 342 readings to a median of 0.17 decibels -- agreeing with the broadband balance to a tenth through the middle of the sweep and departing from it by two decibels at the last byte, which is where the broadband reading was reading the added term. The table's two sides are one table read in opposite directions, 0.54 of a decibel apart at worst over 17 settings, and its centre entry sits 2.44 decibels under its end -- neither the 3.01 of a constant-power pair nor the 6.02 of a straight crossfade.

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: A rate byte does not drive a formula. It indexes a printed table of whole steps of a twentieth of a hertz, and there are two such tables, told apart by the range the page prints against the address. The narrow one is 128 entries of 0.05 Hz, from 0.05 to 6.40. The wide one shares those entries as far as 5.00 Hz at setting 99, then steps by 0.10 to 7.00 at 119 and by 0.50 to 10.00 at 125 -- 126 entries, so the last two settings of the byte have no entry of their own and return the last one. One table serves every type: the same twenty-one slots across nineteen effect types answer to it with no per-type constant anywhere.

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: A gain byte over this type's low shelf does not build the shelf at the gain it names either, and it does not reach it the way the two mid sections of the same type are reached. One shelf is stored at the bottom of the printed range -- the full cut -- and the byte blends the dry path towards that, with a boost being the same section with its numerator and its denominator exchanged. In coefficients it is the same three multiply-accumulates the mid sections use, moved from the numerator to the denominator, and the two are not the same curve: the mid reading has the low shelf falling away half an octave sooner in the middle of the window than the unit does, and this one is out by a quarter of a band.
inferences.named: section-gain

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: A gain byte over a peaking section does not build the section at the gain it names. One section is stored at the top of the printed range and the byte blends it against the dry path, and a cut is that same section with its numerator and its denominator exchanged. The two readings agree at both ends of the window and at its centre and nowhere between, which is why nothing in this archive had noticed: at six decibels of a twelve decibel range the peak is about forty per cent narrower than the width byte asked for, and it is the width and not the height that says so -- every candidate here stands where the byte asked.
inferences.named: section-gain

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: An effect parameter whose page prints a list of states takes no byte that is not one of them, and what it does instead is nothing: the parameter goes on sounding the state it was already in. The store is not what refuses -- it keeps every seven-bit value and reads it back, 02 for a write of 02 -- so whatever drops the value sits between the store and the sound. Read on five two-state slots across three of the effect map's high bytes, where nought against one is audible by 11.74 to 15.49 dB of level and one against two, one against 127 and nought against two are all null -- fifteen pairs whose two settings sit between 2.94 dB under and 0.27 dB over the yardstick those settings' own repeats set, against the 6 dB a verdict here has to clear, and none of which moves the level by more than 0.02 dB. The last of those three pairs is the one that decides it: four of the five slots power up in the second state, so a byte that reached the state they power up in would have made nought against two as loud as nought against one. Three printed lists of different lengths agree -- a two-state corner holds at the 1 it had, a three-state amp table and a five-state width both hold at the 0 they had. Those three were all asked on slots that power up at the first entry, where holding what they had and folding to the first are one number, so every length this page prints was then asked again on a slot that powers up inside its own list: a three-state filter selector and a four-state amp table that power up at 1, and a five-state width inside a multi-effect that powers up at 2. Each was asked one past its top three times over -- standing at nought, standing at the value it powers up in, and standing at its last printed state -- and the three readings that a longer list leaves standing each predict a different two of those three to be audible. All nine are null, between 3.79 dB under and 0.87 dB over the yardstick their own settings' repeats set, while the nine in-range pairs of the same three slots are audible by 16.08 to 38.17 dB over theirs. None of the three moves again further up: nought against 127 and the last printed state against 127 are null on each. Eight of the fifty-four slots printed `00/01` now carry it, over eight types including a delay line, a distortion and three guitar multi-effects, each audible at nought against one by 25.66 dB or more and null at nought against two. And the four slots the page prints `00/7F` are not a longer or shorter case of this but a different thing entirely: each was swept over the whole byte with the type reloaded before every take, so what comes back is a function of the byte alone -- the slow rotor from nought to 63 and the fast one from 64 to 127 -- while a slot printed `00/01` returns two different states for the one byte 2 depending on which state it was standing in. No map from a byte to a state does both.

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: A delay-time byte does not scale a time and does not run a formula. It indexes a ladder of round decimal milliseconds whose step changes a few times over the byte, and every entry is then cut back to a whole step of a clock running at 32000 Hz -- which is what a delay addressed as a sample count does to a time written in milliseconds. Which ladder a slot is on is picked by the conversion column the effect list cites beside it, not by the range the page prints -- two slots print the same range and cite different columns, and they return ladders fifty milliseconds apart. On 0 - 500m the step is a tenth of a millisecond to setting fifty, then a half to sixty, then one to ninety, then ten to a hundred and sixteen, then twenty to a hundred and twenty-six; on 0 - 100m it is the same tenth to fifty and half to sixty, then one to a hundred, then two to a hundred and twenty-five; on 200m - 990m/1sec the byte starts at two hundred milliseconds and steps five to setting seventy, then ten to a hundred and fifteen, where it reaches one second; on 0m - 635m the step never changes at all -- five milliseconds from the first setting to the last; and 0m - 500m, which the page spells with an m the other five-hundred range does not have, is that range's ladder entry for entry. Four of the five reach the printed end before the byte ends and repeat it at every setting above, and the fifth reaches it at its last setting, so where a ladder stops is read off the record in both directions. The cut is not a detail of the ladder: it is what the settings at the short end actually return, and it is what decides which settings the reading brings back a tall peak for. It is also why two of the five ranges say nothing about the clock -- every entry on them is five milliseconds or more, which is already a whole step of it, so there is no setting at which the two readings differ. One slot of the five does not read its ladder from wherever it is asked. On the type whose delay glides, a setting reached from below is short of its cited column by a thousand and sixteen whole samples of the same clock, and the same setting reached from above returns that column times a hundred and twenty-seven over a hundred and twenty-eight exactly -- the same one-byte ratio every entry here carries. So the shortfall the sweep found is the sweep's own direction and not a second regime in the table, and the byte the page prints beside it as an acceleration is worth exactly half of it, from its top bit alone and from no other bit in the nibble. The ladder a column picks is the same ladder at every address that cites it. One type prints four of these rows at four addresses, three of which nothing in this class had been read at, and prints a different default against each -- 500ms, 300ms, 400ms, 200ms -- where the conversion column is one column for all four. All four return the ladder read on the type beside it, to within 0.042 ms at every setting either was asked at, against a floor of 0.0834 ms on the noisiest of them and 0.0 on the other three. So the printed default is not what picks a ladder either, which the page gives no other way to tell. A column's ladder does not change for what stands in front of the delay either. Four types that print this row put another stage before or beside it -- an enhancer, a chorus in front, a chorus beside, a flanger beside -- and every one of them returns the ladder its column was read on, to within 0.000 ms at all eight settings asked of each, on a reading quantised to 0.020833 ms. Two more print it behind a waveshaper and are not read here, for a reason that is about the reading and not about the byte.

inferences.why: reproduces
inferences.claim: The tone controls these two types carry are one pair of first-order shelves whose corners are fixed and have no byte: a low shelf near 161 Hz and a high shelf near 6987 Hz, each of them a point inside a range these readings leave open rather than a number they resolve. The pair is the same pair on both types -- fitted to each type on its own the low corners land 0.0 octaves apart and the high ones 0.0119, and one shared pair scores each record as well as its own fit does. The section is one pole and one zero: a unit-slope second-order shelf is two to three times worse on the median of every one of the four records and three times worse at its worst, and its worst band is in the shelf's own transition every time. The gain is not fitted here at all -- it is the window the gain class closed on, twenty-five values centred on 64 that stick at both ends, and the same window that type 01 00 was read with. Six front halves carry one pair, and the corner is a range and not a number. Four further front halves were swept at the same two addresses, chosen for having nothing in common with the first two or with each other: 01 02 (a generator of harmonics with nothing summed in), 01 20 (eight all-pass sections turned down to the dry signal), 01 25 (an amplitude modulator at no depth), 02 06 (two blocks in series). The pair reproduces all four to a median of 0.160 dB or better against spans of twenty decibels and more, worst band 4.78 dB, and the second-order pair is beaten on every record the same way it was beaten before -- its best worst band anywhere in the six is 6.22 dB and it is inside the shelf's own transition every time. Three of the four carry no balance byte at all, so on those there is no direct half to park and what reached the gains is what the front half passed. **The corner is a range, and the round that closed this claim published it as a number.** Scanned over five octaves rather than refined around one grid point, every corner between 112 and 161 Hz fits the low shelf inside every record's own floor: those widths run to 1.55 octaves and the narrowest is 0.52. The high side has been read twice since -- once through a shelf whose half-gain point is where its parameter says it is, and once on a grid 25 times finer than the one that found it -- and it comes back 6872 to 7240 Hz, a band of 5.4 per cent shared by the five records whose own floors close on it. It is far narrower than it was and it is still a range. The two corners the model carries sit inside those ranges and are kept, because nothing measured moves them and a second point estimate would be the same artefact with a different value. What the agreement between types is worth is that no type's range sits outside the others' -- which is what was being asked, and is now asked of six.
inferences.named: a fixed first-order shelf pair, the part's tone control

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: A modulation wave byte indexes five fixed shapes and computes nothing, and four of the five are the shapes the page names them. Read on two types that drive different quantities with the same byte -- one swinging its output's level by more than the whole of its own mean, the other swinging the balance between its channels by forty decibels -- the entry printed `Tri` returns a triangle, `Sqr` a square and `Saw1` and `Saw2` a sawtooth, each nearer the shape it is named after than any other by both of the two readings taken, on both types, 8 readings out of 8. `Saw1` and `Saw2` are one shape run two ways: no reading of magnitudes can separate them, which the two candidates sitting exactly zero apart under both scores says outright, and what separates them is that one spends nine tenths of its cycle climbing and the other one tenth. The fifth entry is not what it is printed. `Sin` carries a third harmonic of four to six hundredths where a sine has none and a triangle has a ninth, and a fifth harmonic of two thousandths where a triangle has a twenty-fifth -- so it is neither, and it is a sine made cheaply. Which cheap sine is not settled and is queued. The shape is a shape of a multiplier and not of a level: the same cycles come back clean read in amplitude and warped read in decibels, which is what a gain swung linearly does to a logarithm and not what a gain swung in decibels would do to either. Three readings stood against this and each had a run; all three ran. The five shapes are not these two types': the third place the same five names are printed returns the same five, entry for entry, no further apart than 0.0122 in any harmonic either reading carries, with both sawtooths climbing the same way round. The depth byte scales the cycle rather than reshaping it, and what looked like a shape moving with depth was the reading's own logarithm: read as a difference between two channels in decibels the third harmonic sits a median 0.0582 from the linear reading at the top of the byte and 0.0166 at a quarter of it, converging on it as the swing shrinks and the logarithm straightens. And the entry printed `Sin` is not the parabola. It is not the parabola, and it is refused from both sides at once. Rendered onto one of this unit's own takes and read back through the whole stage, the parabola returns a third harmonic of 0.0409 where the unit returns 0.0600, and a fifth of 0.0054 where the unit returns 0.0029 -- too little of the one and more than twice too much of the other, which no scaling of a candidate can fix in both directions at once. What fits is a sine carrying a small third harmonic and almost nothing above it: a sine carrying a fifteenth of its third lands 0.0038 away where the parabola lands 0.0112, 3.0 times as far. That is a description of the cycle and not a name for what makes it, and this file does not give it one.
inferences.named: a table of five fixed modulator shapes, indexed by a byte, multiplying

inferences.why: equivalent_under_this_test
inferences.claim: A width byte does not hold the number the page prints against it. It indexes five entries and they are the printed figures halved -- 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.5 -- put into the section as the width its bandwidth is defined by at the half-gain points, which is the form the era's filter arithmetic is written in. Settings past the fifth return what the first returns, which on this slot is also the entry it powers up in, so the two cannot be told apart from these takes. A fourth type carrying the same printed table tells them apart by disagreeing with both: its byte powers up at the third entry and everything past the fifth returns the fifth, so which entry a byte outside the printed steps comes back at is a property of the slot and not of the table. The five entries do not depend on where the peak is: the same table answers with the centre at the bottom of its own table and with it in the middle, and the two mid sections of the type answer alike.
inferences.named: filter-width
